I'm 78 years old, been farming these 5 mu in Quzhou for 55 years. Didn't go to school much — just a few years of primary — but I know this land better than any book. My son and his wife work over in Handan at a factory, send some money back when they can. My wife and I do what we're able, and my grandson helps on weekends when he's not studying. We've got six mouths to feed, so every yuan matters.

I split my 5 mu the same way I always have: 3 mu for wheat then maize, and 2 mu for cotton. The wheat and maize keep us in grain and feed the pigs. The cotton gives us cash for fertilizer and school fees.

The wheat went in last October, local seed I saved from the year before. No point buying new seed when mine grows fine. I put down base fertilizer then — about half a bag of compound fertilizer per mu, and some urea. Now it's spring, the wheat is growing fast. I already topdressed with urea at green-up, about 8 kg per mu. I'll irrigate two more times before June harvest if the weather stays dry. My neighbor Old Wang irrigates four times, but the pump electricity costs too much. Last year I got about 400 kg per mu, hoping for the same.

For cotton, I'm planting right now, mid-April. Bought the seed from the village supply shop — the kind Old Wang uses, about 40 yuan for the seed per mu. I work the soil good in spring, make furrows, put fertilizer in the holes when I plant. Cotton needs weeding and spraying when the bugs come. I'll irrigate once or twice if the rain doesn't come.

Then in mid-June, right after we cut the wheat, we plant the maize. No time to waste — the window is tight, maybe five days. I hire the combine for wheat harvest now, my back can't handle the scythe anymore. For maize I buy hybrid seed, about 3 kg per mu. Put compound fertilizer down at planting, then topdress with urea when the plants are knee-high. Maybe irrigate once or twice.

Money is tight. My pension is only a little over 100 yuan a month. I can't throw fertilizer around like those big business farms. But I also know that if I cut back too much, the crop fails and we're in real trouble. So I do what I've always done — it's not fancy, but it's enough to get by.
